text: Portal, Theme, and Page are the configuration layers, but none of them actually render content. The thing that renders content, placed on a Page, is a Widget — stored on the sp_widget table. Every widget is built from exactly four parts: an HTML Template, CSS, a Server Script, and a Client Controller.

The Server Script is where the GlideRecord skills from earlier in this course get used inside Service Portal. It runs server-side, queries whatever table the widget needs — here, open incidents for the logged-in caller, using gs dot getUserID — and pushes the results into a data object. Every field pushed has to be a plain value, a string or number, because a raw GlideRecord object can't cross from server script to client. That's why the script calls getValue instead of handing back the record itself.

The HTML Template reads that data through ng-repeat, the AngularJS directive that loops the markup once per element in the array. Here, ng-repeat equals inc in c dot data dot incidents renders one list item per open incident, and double-curly interpolation — inc dot number, inc dot short underscore description — drops each value straight into the page.

The Client Controller is plain AngularJS-style JavaScript. Service Portal widgets commonly use the controller-as pattern, where c is the alias referenced in the HTML — c dot data, c dot openIncident. Scope is injected because AngularJS controllers always receive it, even when most of the logic hangs off c instead. c dot data is populated automatically from the Server Script's output — no manual wiring required.

c dot openIncident is a plain function the HTML's ng-click calls directly when the View button is clicked — in this example, navigating to the ticket's detail page using spNavigator and the incident's sys_id.

Building a widget follows that same order every time: write the Server Script first so you know what data looks like, then write the HTML Template to render it, then write the Client Controller to wire up any interactive behavior the template needs.

Once built, an implementer drags the widget onto a target Page's layout in the page designer. The same widget record behaves identically wherever it's dropped, because it's one sp_widget record, configured once. Next up: the lab, building a complete My Open Requests widget end to end.
